summary: This informational document registers media types used by the Cloud Data Management Interface, a cloud storage interface from the Storage Networking Industry Association. The types name the kinds of objects it works with, such as objects, containers, domains, capabilities, and queues. It is not a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A cloud storage system handles different kinds of things, like files and folders. This document gives each kind an official label so programs know what they are receiving.

questions: cloud data management interface media types
subtitle: Register media types for cloud storage objects, containers, and metadata.

tldr.problem: The Cloud Data Management Interface (CDMI) is a standardized API for cloud storage that works with several kinds of objects (files, folders, queues, domains, capabilities), but lacked MIME media types to identify them when transmitted over HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers five media types with IANA to represent the different CDMI object kinds: application/cdmi-object, application/cdmi-container, application/cdmi-domain, application/cdmi-capability, and application/cdmi-queue.
tldr.outcome: HTTP clients and servers can now correctly identify and process CDMI objects by their media type, enabling standards-compliant cloud storage APIs.

today: RFC 6208 remains current as the authoritative registration of MIME media types for CDMI objects. CDMI is used by several cloud storage providers and is a key specification in the SNIA portfolio for standardized cloud storage APIs.

sections.title: Cloud Storage and CDMI
sections.content:
The Cloud Data Management Interface (CDMI), created by the Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA), is a functional API that applications use to create, retrieve, update, and delete data in a storage cloud. A storage cloud pools resources that are allocated on demand, smaller increments than traditional equipment purchase. The CDMI defines both data paths (how applications read and write) and management interfaces (how to configure storage and metadata).

A key concept in CDMI is metadata, which lets applications specify requirements (performance, retention, encryption) that the cloud service can use to differentiate how it treats each piece of data. The CDMI also defines an extensible metadata system and a capabilities mechanism that lets clients discover what features a cloud provider supports.
sections.plainLanguage: A cloud storage service is like a big digital warehouse. Different things go in it: files, folders, job queues, administrative settings, and information about what the warehouse can do. This document names each kind of thing.

sections.title: CDMI Object Hierarchy
sections.content:
CDMI defines a storage hierarchy with five kinds of objects:

Objects: The basic storage element, analogous to a file in a filesystem. An object is represented in JSON format with a single value field and optional metadata. Implementations can store the actual data however they choose, but present it as a CDMI object.

Containers: Groups of stored data, analogous to a directory. A container can hold zero or more child objects and other containers (forming a tree), and includes standardized and custom metadata fields.

Queues: A special kind of container that implements first-in, first-out semantics. Writers PUT objects into a queue, and readers GET and acknowledge them. Queues provide a simple reliable way for one or more writers to send data to a single reader.

Domains: Administrative units representing logical ownership of stored data. Domains form a hierarchy and are used to map access control lists to principals and to aggregate billing and usage data.

Capabilities: A special read-only container that lets clients discover which subset of the CDMI standard the provider implements. For each URI, the set of named capabilities describes what operations the system supports.
sections.plainLanguage: Objects are files. Containers are folders. Queues are ordered job lists. Domains are departments. Capabilities are 'here is what I can do' labels.

sections.title: Five CDMI Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers five media types to represent these CDMI objects:

application/cdmi-object: Represents a single data object with a value and optional metadata in JSON format. This is the primary type for data storage.

application/cdmi-container: Represents a container (directory-like) object with child objects and metadata. Containers can nest other containers.

application/cdmi-domain: Represents a domain object, which groups stored data for administrative purposes and access control. Domains form a hierarchy.

application/cdmi-capability: A read-only container describing the capabilities of a CDMI provider. Capabilities are always static and tell clients what operations are supported at each URI.

application/cdmi-queue: Represents a queue object with FIFO semantics. Queue objects are created and managed like regular data objects but support FIFO access.

All CDMI objects are transmitted over HTTP (CDMI does not operate over other protocols), and each media type designation allows clients and servers to correctly identify and process the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label tells a program: 'this is a file', 'this is a folder', 'this is a job queue', 'this is an administrative group', or 'this is a list of what I can do'.

sections.title: Security and Operational Concerns
sections.content:
CDMI media types carry the same security considerations as JSON and XML. Confidentiality and integrity of CDMI objects MUST be protected using HTTPS and authentication mechanisms. Access control is enforced at the CDMI provider level: the media type itself carries no access information.

CDMI includes audit logging capabilities so that administrators can track who accessed what data. Implementations MUST carefully validate JSON input to prevent injection attacks and denial-of-service attacks (such as extremely large objects or deeply nested structures). Additionally, because JSON can carry executable code in some contexts, CDMI implementations must not execute code from received objects.

The RFC notes that metadata in CDMI is user-extensible, so implementations should validate custom metadata and ensure it does not conflict with system metadata or bypass security controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Cloud storage must be encrypted, checked for tampering, and kept from unauthorized access. Programs must be careful not to trust that a received object is what it claims.
